transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?
I’m here because once I start worrying, I can’t really turn it off. I’ll make a list, check the dates, do what I can, but my mind just keeps going over it anyway.
What kinds of things do you find yourself worrying about the most?

It can be all sorts of things. The exhibition schedule, my daughter’s travel plans, whether the gutters on the house need fixing. My mind just moves from one thing to the next, and little concerns start feeling like they could turn into something much bigger.
How long have you been experiencing this persistent worrying?
About seven months now. It started not long after my friend died, when I was trying to keep our projects moving along.
Before your friend passed away, were you also prone to this kind of persistent worrying, or is this completely new for you?
I’m not really sure. I think I worried about ordinary things before, but not in this way where it keeps circling and I can’t let it go.
Have you noticed physical tension in your muscles, like stiffness or tightness, when you feel this way?

Yes. By the evening my shoulders and neck feel very tight, like I’ve been holding myself braced all day. I also notice I’m clenching my jaw when I’m reading or planning activities for the garden center.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep, such as trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?
I’m not sure I’ve noticed any real change in my sleep.
Do you often feel restless, keyed up, or on edge?
Yes, I do. Even at home I feel sort of wound up—I’ll tap my fingers during phone calls or get up and straighten something because sitting still makes me feel jumpy.
Have you found that you tire easily or feel unusually worn out during the day?

Yes. Even when I sleep through the night, I wake up feeling like I’ve already put in half a day. By the time I’ve watered the garden beds or sorted papers for book club, I usually need to sit down and gather myself.
